summary: This document describes using Bidirectional Forwarding Detection in point-to-point Geneve unicast tunnels that make up an overlay network. BFD quickly detects when a path between two endpoints fails.

eli5.summary: Two friends on each end of a tunnel keep waving to each other. If one stops waving, the other knows something is wrong right away.

questions: how does bfd work over geneve tunnels
what ttl does bfd use in geneve
subtitle: How two Geneve tunnel endpoints use BFD to notice quickly when the path between them stops working.

tldr.problem: Geneve tunnels build overlay networks, but the two tunnel endpoints need a fast way to tell whether the path between them is still working.
tldr.mechanism: BFD Control packets in asynchronous mode are carried inside the Geneve tunnel, either inside an inner Ethernet/IP/UDP packet or an inner IP/UDP packet, with fixed header values so the receiver can pick out the right BFD session.
tldr.outcome: Operators get continuity monitoring for point-to-point Geneve tunnels, with the rule that BFD for Geneve must run inside a Traffic-Managed Controlled Environment unless BFD is truly congestion controlled.

today: RFC 9521 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2024. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why BFD for Geneve
sections.content:
Geneve (RFC 8926) lets operators build an overlay network of tunnels, decoupling the address space of attached virtual hosts from that of the network. Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD, RFC 5880) is a protocol for monitoring whether a path between two systems is still alive.

RFC 9521 describes how to run BFD between two Geneve tunnel endpoints, which may be a Network Virtualization Edge (NVE) or another device acting as an endpoint. Only the asynchronous mode of BFD is used, and only for point-to-point (P2P) Geneve tunnels. The BFD Echo function is outside the scope of the document.

The use cases and deployment are mostly consistent with those of BFD for VXLAN in RFC 8971. One exception is the Management Virtual Network Identifier (VNI), which is left to a separate work in progress.
sections.eli5: A tunnel can quietly break without anyone noticing. This document says how the two ends of a Geneve tunnel keep checking on each other so a break is spotted fast.

sections.title: Terms: NVE, Tenant System and VAP
sections.content:
The RFC uses an NVE to stand for any Geneve tunnel endpoint. A Tenant System (TS) is the physical or virtual device attached to a tunnel endpoint from the outside. A Virtual Access Point (VAP) is the NVE side of the interface between the NVE and the TS: a logical network port, virtual or physical, into a specific virtual network.

The BFD session is originated and terminated at a VAP of an NVE, not at the NVE as a whole. Detailed definitions are left to RFC 7365 and RFC 8014.
sections.eli5: Think of an NVE as an apartment building and each VAP as one front door into one of its private hallways. The BFD chat happens door to door.

sections.title: BFD in an Inner Ethernet/IP/UDP Packet
sections.content:
Geneve payloads can be either Ethernet frames or IP packets, so the RFC defines two encapsulations. The choice follows how the originating VAP encapsulates its data packets. If the VAP carries Ethernet, the BFD Control packet rides in an inner Ethernet frame, over IP, over UDP.

The outer IP/UDP and Geneve headers are encoded as in RFC 8926. The outer and inner IP headers need not be the same address family, so an outer IPv6 header with an inner IPv4 header is allowed, and the reverse as well.

For the inner headers, the destination MAC is the MAC address of a VAP of the terminating NVE and the source MAC is that of the originating NVE. The source and destination IP addresses are those of the VAPs. If a VAP has no IP address, the source uses 0.0.0.0 (IPv4) or ::/128 (IPv6), and the destination uses 127.0.0.1 (IPv4) or ::1/128 (IPv6). The TTL or Hop Limit MUST be 255, as in the single-hop BFD of RFC 5881, which also defines the UDP and BFD Control fields.

The Geneve header values are fixed: the O bit MUST be 1 (a control message), the C bit MUST be 0 (no critical option), the Protocol Type MUST be 0x6558 (Ethernet frame), and the VNI MUST be the one the originating VAP is mapped to. Opt Len is set as usual, and the use of Geneve options with BFD is out of scope.
sections.eli5: When the tunnel carries whole Ethernet frames, the BFD message is wrapped like a letter in an envelope, inside a bigger envelope, inside the tunnel. Each envelope has its labels filled in a set way.

sections.title: BFD in an Inner IP/UDP Packet
sections.content:
If the originating VAP encapsulates IP data packets, the BFD Control packet is carried directly in an inner IP packet over UDP, with no inner Ethernet header. Source and destination IP are the addresses of the originating and terminating VAPs, and TTL or Hop Limit MUST again be 255. UDP and BFD fields follow RFC 5881.

The Geneve header rules match the Ethernet case, except for the Protocol Type: it MUST be 0x0800 for an inner IPv4 packet or 0x86DD for an inner IPv6 packet. The O bit is 1, the C bit is 0, and the VNI is the one the originating VAP is mapped to.
sections.eli5: Here the tunnel carries plain IP letters, so the BFD message needs one less envelope. Only the type label on the tunnel header changes.

sections.title: Demultiplexing Received BFD Packets
sections.content:
A receiving NVE first validates the packet as RFC 8926 requires. For an Ethernet payload it checks that the Protocol Type is 0x6558 and that the inner destination MAC matches a VAP mapped to the received VNI. It then validates the inner destination IP, the UDP destination port and the TTL or Hop Limit. For an IP payload the Protocol Type is 0x0800 or 0x86DD, and the checks cover the destination IP, UDP port and TTL or Hop Limit. If validation fails, the packet MUST NOT be processed by BFD.

One NVE usually owns several VAPs, and RFC 8014 allows N-to-1 mapping between VAPs and VNIs, so several BFD sessions can exist between the same two NVEs, even for the same VNI. A session can only be established between two VAPs mapped to the same VNI that encapsulate data the same way.

To find the right session, the rules depend on the Your Discriminator field. If it is 0, the session SHOULD be identified by the VNI plus the inner headers (source and destination MAC and IP for Ethernet, source and destination IP for IP). An implementation MAY also use the inner UDP source port. If no session is found, the packet MUST be dropped and an exception event should be reported to management. If Your Discriminator is non-zero, the session MUST be demultiplexed using only that value as the key.
sections.eli5: Many pairs of doors may be chatting through the same tunnel. The receiver looks at the labels, or at a ticket number if there is one, to know which chat each message belongs to.

sections.title: Congestion and Security
sections.content:
Geneve MUST be used with congestion-controlled traffic or inside a Traffic-Managed Controlled Environment (TMCE), and this also applies to BFD traffic. Because the BFD congestion control mechanism is considered complex and immature, BFD for Geneve MUST be used within a TMCE unless BFD is really congestion controlled. As an alternative, a TMCE operator is required to provision the BFD transmission rates to avoid congestion and false failure detection.

Security issues from RFC 8926 and RFC 5880 apply. Since Geneve has no inherent security mechanisms, BFD authentication as in RFC 5880 is RECOMMENDED. The document also warns about session overload: with N VAPs on each of two NVEs using Ethernet payloads, there could be N squared BFD sessions. There SHOULD be a mechanism to limit how many are active, and running N sessions that cover all the VAPs is recommended instead.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Too many check-in calls can clog the line, so the rules say to keep them under control. And since the tunnel has no lock of its own, use BFD's password feature.
